titre_video: Why Ancient Human Drug Use Was 10x More Lethal Than Today

segments.titre: Hook: Greek civilization built on a psychedelic ritual
segments.resume: The video opens by claiming that Athens' greatest minds were powered by a state-sponsored, elite-enforced psychedelic ritual rather than pure logic. The ritual is presented as a chemical designed to control the masses and hidden for 2,000 years.
segments.texte: Everything we know about the birth of Western civilization is a lie. The Ancient Greeks built modern society on nothing but logic and reason. But the truth is much darker. Athens’ greatest minds were actually powered by a state-sponsored, elite-enforced psychedelic ritual. It wasn’t accidental foraging. It was a highly sophisticated chemical that was designed to suppress the masses. And it’s been hiding in plain sight for 2,000 years.

segments.titre: Eleusinian Mysteries: secrecy and entry rules
segments.resume: The ruling elites of Athens guarded the ritual under penalty of death. It took place at Eleusis, 13 miles northwest of Athens, and participants could not be murderers and had to speak and understand Greek.
segments.texte: The ruling elites of Athens guarded the secretive nature of the ritual with an iron fist. Revealing any details was punishable by death. To even get a taste of it, some of the greatest minds in history had to endure a gruelling, physical gauntlet known as the mysteries. It all took place in a city 13 miles (21 km) northwest of Athens called Eleusis. There were two general requirements to even take part in for the mysteries: participants couldn’t have any blood on their hands - so murderers were out - and they had to speak and understand Greek.

segments.titre: The ordeal: Sacred Way, fasting and the kykeon cup
segments.resume: Participants walked the Sacred Way honoring the myth of Demeter and Persephone, which centers on death and rebirth. After bathing, animal sacrifices and a 9 day fast, weakened participants were handed a cup of a secret brew called kykeon.
segments.texte: Then the true ordeal began. The participants were forced to trek through “The Sacred Way”, a path that honored the story of Demeter and Persephone. It wasn’t a coincidence. The myth of Persephone focused on death and rebirth, slipping between the underworld and life on earth. This procession was followed by bathing and animal sacrifices. Then, they undertook a 9 day fast. Once they were weak, broken and pushed to the brink, the participants were allowed to break their fast. They were handed a cup containing a secretive brew. Kykeon.

segments.titre: Kykeon spiked with ergot
segments.resume: Kykeon was an ordinary peasant drink of barley, water and mint given to infantrymen, but the version at Eleusis contained a secret ingredient guarded by priestesses. Scholars think it was ergot, a parasitic fungus on barley that is the natural starting point for LSD.
segments.texte: To everyday Atheneans, it wasn’t anything special. It was a regular peasant drink made from barley, water and mint. It was handed out to infantrymen every day. But the kykeon handed out in Eleusis was different. It was spiked with another special ingredient. One that was closely guarded by the priestesses Today, scholars think that barley was hiding a little surprise: a parasitic fungus known as ergot. Nature’s starting point for LSD.

segments.titre: Wasson and Hofmann: ergot, LSD and ancient philosophers
segments.resume: Because participants were sworn to secrecy, what happened is unknown, but research by Gordon Wasson and Albert Hofmann shows what ergot does to the brain. Hofmann created LSD while working with ergot alkaloids, suggesting ancient thinkers took an ancient variation of it.
segments.texte: Because of the strict rules surrounding the mysteries, no one really knows what took place. Participants were sworn to secrecy.Because the priestesses would not let the secret out. However, thanks to research by scientists Gordon Wasson and Albert Hofmann, we know what the ergot fungus does to the human brain. Hofmann was working with the ergot alkaloids when he accidentally created the LSD. Which means some of the best ancient philosophers, playwrights, and military strategists in history were dosing it as well. Or at least an ancient variation of it. So what happened when they took it?

segments.titre: Reported effects: preview of death and fearlessness
segments.resume: Greeks and Romans such as Plato, Cicero and Marcus Aurelius were said to have had life-changing experiences at the mysteries. Leaked details describe a transcendent preview of death and a new fearlessness about dying afterwards.
segments.texte: Greeks and Romans like Plato, Cicero, and Marcus Aurelius had profound, life-changing experiences during the mysteries, thanks in part to kykeon. A few details of the mysteries did leak over time. Participants talked about seeing a transcendent preview of death, and then were said to leave the experience with a new fearlessness about death itself.

segments.titre: Skeptics and the lye detox of ergot
segments.resume: Skeptics argue raw ergot is a deadly toxin that would have killed the philosophers without modern lab equipment. Tests showed that treating ergot with water and wood ash lye removed the danger while keeping the hallucinogenic properties.
segments.texte: But skeptics completely dismiss this theory. Ergot in its rawest form is a deadly toxin. Without modern lab equipment, the philosophers of the Eleusinian Mysteries wouldn’t just have a life-altering revelation. They’d suffer an agonizing death. But scientists went a step further. Running tests, they found that using simple ancient techniques, like treating ergot with water and wood ashes - or lye - removed its potential danger. But it still kept the hallucinogenic and mind-altering properties intact. So were history’s greatest thinkers tripping? New evidence suggests that’s the case.

segments.titre: Girona temple evidence: ancient master chemists
segments.resume: A temple to two Eleusinian goddesses near Girona, Spain yielded a vase with ergot remnants and the skeleton of a 25-year-old man showing ergot consumption. This supports the view that ancient people engineered sophisticated pharmaceutical-grade tools to gatekeep power, war and divine revelation.
segments.texte: A temple dedicated to two Eleusinian goddesses was discovered near Girona, Spain. The excavation discovered a vase at the temple with the remnants of ergot in it. But they also found the skeleton of a 25-year-old man that showed he had consumed ergot. It’s just one of many indications that ancient people were not primitive when it came to herbs and substances. They were more like master chemists who engineered sophisticated pharmaceutical-grade biological tools to gatekeep power, war, and divine revelation.

segments.titre: 90% of societies used altered states, but access was gatekept
segments.resume: A cross-cultural survey of 488 old world societies found about 90% had institutionalized altered states of consciousness, comparable to caffeine, nicotine and alcohol today. Unlike today, when anyone can get a beer or coffee, these substances were reserved for an elite few according to the ruling classes' needs.
segments.texte: Ancient Greece isn’t the only example. One cross-cultural survey found that, among 488 societies in the old world, around 90% of these groups had some institutionalized forms of altered states of consciousness. The academics studying the topic found that “the ubiquity of mind-altering agents in traditional societies cannot be doubted - just as the moods of industrial societies are set by a balance of caffeine, nicotine and alcohol”. But there’s a massive difference between then and now. Almost anyone today can get a beer or a cup of coffee. But societies gatekept these substances for an elite few, depending on what the ruling classes needed from them.

segments.titre: Viking berserkers: trance-like rage in battle
segments.resume: The Norse berserkers, described in the Saga period (about 870 to 1030 AD) and by Snorri Sturluson as mad as dogs or wolves and strong as bears, fought in a trance-like blind rage, howling and biting their shields. They sometimes attacked fellow Vikings, unable to tell friend from enemy.
segments.texte: Like the Vikings. Viking warriors were feared around the old world for the devastation, looting, and violence they left in their wake. But there was a particular type of Viking feared much more than the others: The Norse “berserker”. Accounts of them are found all throughout the Viking Saga period, roughly between 870 and 1030 AD. Icelandic poet Snorri Sturluson called them “mad as dogs or wolves” and “strong as bears or wild oxen”. They seemed to be superhuman. They would enter battle in a state that was often described as trance-like. Charging in with a blind rage, the Berserkers would howl like animals and biting their shields. They sometimes attacked their fellow Vikings because they lost the ability to distinguish between friends and enemies. Their strength was immense; no one could go up against them.

segments.titre: Berserkers' pain immunity and the drug hypothesis
segments.resume: Berserkers seemed almost immune to pain and barely bled when cut, which hinted to ethnobotanist Karsten Fatur of the University of Ljubljana that a drug was involved. The idea is a substance driving men into rage that leaders could dose at the right moment to guarantee victory.
segments.texte: Even more terrifying, they seemed almost immune to injury and pain. It was reported they would barely even bleed when injured with blades. One historical account could be an exaggeration… but all of them? Ethnobotanist Karsten Fatur, of the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia, suspected more was at play. Specifically, a drug. A dangerous substance that drove men insane with rage; but one that Viking leaders could utilize to their advantage. A dose given at just the right time to almost guarantee victory in battle.

segments.titre: Henbane and the phases of berserkergana
segments.resume: Fatur believes the drug was Hyoscyamus niger, henbane. The onset of berserkergana began with chills, shivering and teeth chattering, then swelling and reddening of the face, then rage, followed by days of fatigue and emotional numbness.
segments.texte: Fatur believes it was Hyoscyamus niger. Otherwise known as henbane. Apparently the onset of “berserkergana” began with “bodily chills, shivering, and teeth chattering, followed by swelling and reddening of the face. Then the rage broke out… once it abated, the berserker would experience… physical fatigue and emotional numbness for a few days.”

segments.titre: Narrowing down the plant: native black henbane
segments.resume: Fatur compared the symptoms against possible herbs and plants, since mushrooms were suggested by many scientists but did not explain everything, especially the lack of bleeding. Few plants in Scandinavia today are native, but black henbane is, a weed found everywhere.
segments.texte: Reading through these strange symptoms, and the almost superhuman strength of the Viking warriors, Fatur started narrowing down possible herbs and plants. Many scientists thought it might be a type of mushroom causing these symptoms. But it didn’t explain everything. Especially the lack of bleeding people saw when berserkers were hit. Fatur’s research was helped by the fact that few plants and herbs grown in Scandinavia today are actually native to the region. But he discovered one that was; a weed that was found everywhere. The black henbane. It causes a huge array of symptoms in humans.

segments.titre: How henbane explains berserker traits: the biological tank
segments.resume: Henbane dulls pain, impairs recognition of faces (explaining attacks on their own men), lowers blood pressure (explaining little bleeding) and causes rage depending on dosage and mental set. The mindset of men about to raid a village intensified the effect, creating a super soldier or biological tank.
segments.texte: Like dulling pain. That would explain why the berserkers didn’t seem to register hits like normal warriors. It also confuses the brain’s ability to recognize faces. Something that might explain why the berserkers would sometimes attack their own men. Henbane also lowers blood pressure which would point to the lack of bleeding. Of course, the main symptom was the reason why leaders gave it to their men in the first place: rage. As Fatur writes: “this anger effect can range from agitation to full-blown rage and combativeness depending on the dosage and mental set.” The mental state of a group of men about to raid and attack a village would only intensify the drug’s “rage” side effect. Essentially, henbane created a “biological tank” in an otherwise low-tech period. A super soldier with significantly reduced pain sensitivity and dissociation.

segments.titre: Blue lotus in Ancient Egypt: euphoria and symbol of immortality
segments.resume: Not all ancient drugs were about violence; the Egyptians used blue lotus for euphoria and healing. The flower is rare and endangered, appears in the Book of the Dead, was found on Tutankhamun's body by Howard Carter in 1922, and symbolized life and immortality.
segments.texte: Not all drugs in the ancient world were associated with anger and violence though. Some were actually taken for their healing properties. And some were taken to make the users happy…and achieve a feeling of true euphoria. Which is why Ancient Egypt turned to the blue lotus flower. Though many alternative medicine companies are marketing blue lotus today, they’re not actually selling the same thing Egyptians were consuming. The actual flower is actually quite rare, and is considered endangered. The blue lotus was incredibly important to Ancient Egypt. It’s mentioned several times in the Book of the Dead. In 1922, archaeologist Howard Carter found blue lotus petals covering the body of the recently unearthed Tutankhamun. It was found on countless ancient papyri scrolls. It was such an integral party of Ancient Egyptian culture, the blue lotus came to symbolize life and immortality itself.

segments.titre: How the Egyptians used blue lotus with wine
segments.resume: Researchers see blue lotus as a combination of ecstasy and anti-anxiety medication depending on use, though it remains an enigma. Egyptians added it to wine directly or made an infused oil for wine, almost always combined with alcohol for a stronger high.
segments.texte: So what exactly does it do? That’s the strange thing about it. Ancient Egyptians may have been more aware of all its uses and effects than we are today. As one article puts it, “the blue lotus remains an enigma”. But researchers have uncovered some of its uses. As far as they can tell, the blue lotus functioned as some kind of combination of ecstasy and anti-anxiety medication, depending on how it was used. Ancient Egyptians would either add it to wine directly, or make an infused oil from it and add that to wine. It was almost always consumed in combination with alcohol, giving an extra powerful high.

segments.titre: Blue lotus chemistry and medical uses: apomorphine and nuciferine
segments.resume: The active ingredients are apomorphine, a dopamine agonist that induces euphoria, and nuciferine, which acts like an antipsychotic and brings calm. Apomorphine has been used for Parkinson's disease and erectile dysfunction, and researchers think blue lotus may treat anxiety and insomnia.
segments.texte: The flower’s active ingredients are apomorphine and nuciferine. The latter acts like an antipsychotic drug, bringing the user calmness. Researchers still don’t actually know exactly why that is. The effects of apomorphine are more well understood. It works like a dopamine agonist, inducing a sense of euphoria in the user. Scientists have also found it can help with issues as varied as Parkinson’s disease and erectile dysfunction, as it helps with muscle control. And it doesn’t stop there. Researchers believe the blue lotus flower can also treat anxiety, insomnia, and a whole host of other diseases they haven’t discovered yet. But ancient Egyptians were using it more for

segments.resume: Egyptians used blue lotus mostly for its mind-altering properties, as an entheogen or hallucinogen, for religious, medicinal and possibly psychological purposes. Some scholars think elite Egyptians used lotus and wine for hallucinogenic, sex-fueled rituals.
segments.texte: its mind-altering properties than anything else. Because the blue lotus is entheogenic; the scientific way of saying it’s a hallucinogen. IFLScience states the flower was used for “religious, medicinal, and possibly psychological purposes, including treatments for various ailments and psychoactive effects”. segments.titre: Modern blue lotus is far weaker than the ancient flower
segments.resume: Blue lotus sold online today, for example on Etsy, is not the same as what Egyptians consumed; one academic found the endangered ancient species had much higher nuciferine levels. The segment ends by noting ancient people got higher than modern people could guess, especially the Scythians.
segments.texte: sex fueled rituals. The blue lotus sold online today doesn’t hold a candle to the ancient Egyptian version. One academic compared a sample of the endangered species to those sold on places like Etsy. They found that the ancient flower’s nuciferine levels were through the roof compared to the modern version. Ancient people got much higher than the modern population could ever have guessed. That’s probably most true for the Scythians.

segments.titre: Scythians and cannabis: princess grave and soothsayers
segments.resume: The Scythians ruled huge parts of Eurasia for a thousand years yet little is known about them, mostly from Greek and Persian accounts. A container of cannabis in the grave of a 2,500 year old Scythian princess shows its importance in the afterlife, and soothsayers entered trances to predict the future.
segments.texte: Little is known about them compared to other civilizations. That’s despite the fact they ruled huge parts of Eurasia for a thousand years. Most of their history is catalogued by the Greeks and Persians, who lived in fear of them. For years, archaeologists knew that cannabis was important to Scythians. They just didn’t know how much. Archaeologists once found a container of cannabis in a Scythian princess’ grave. She was buried over 2,500 years ago, and the container was among a collection of things she needed in the afterlife. Clearly, the Scythians thought cannabis was such an important personal belonging, it was necessary even in death. The drug also showed up in Scythian religion. Soothsayers entered a trance-like state in order to predict the future for the Scythian people.

segments.titre: Herodotus, the kurgan residue and opium plus cannabis
segments.resume: Herodotus wrote about Scythian cannabis, using it for cloth and for smoke no Grecian vapour-bath could surpass. A Scythian kurgan in southern Russia held golden artifacts with black sticky residue that tested positive for opium and cannabis; Anton Gass and Andrei Belinski believe both were used simultaneously.
segments.texte: Greek historian Herodotus spoke endlessly about the Scythians’ love of cannabis, as well as their drug-fueled exploits. He described them using cannabis to weave their clothes. But he also referred repeatedly to their drug use, saying they used a special plant to make smoke “that no Grecian vapour-bath can surpass.” Archaeologists couldn’t figure out exactly what this substance was. Until the recent discovery of a Scythian kurgan - a grave mound, one the only things Scythians left behind - in southern Russia. They dug up countless golden artifacts. Some of them had an unexpected black, sticky residue inside. Criminologists tested the substance and found a powerful combination: opium and cannabis. Archaeologists Anton Gass and Andrei Belinski believe the ancient Scythians brewed and drank the opium, while the cannabis burned nearby. Or as Gass puts it, “that both drugs were being used simultaneously is beyond doubt.”

segments.titre: Ancient medicine: drugs for pain and surgery, sophisticated processes
segments.resume: Many ancient people got high to dull the pain of diseases that medicine could not cure, and doctors and priests created high-grade compounds. A study by Greek professors found hypnotic drugs used for surgery and cauterization, and drugs produced by drying, grinding, squeezing or boiling roots, often with wine added.
segments.texte: Another reason many ancient people may have gotten high is to dull the pain and symptoms of the diseases that the medicine of the time couldn’t cure. That’s why the doctors and priests of the time created high-grade chemical compounds: to help ancient people get high instead of suffering. One study by Greek professors found that doctors used some drugs’ hypnotic effects for surgical operations and cauterization. Others used drugs that affected the central nervous system for managing severe and chronic painful conditions. These weren’t crude creations. Ancient people weren’t just picking herbs from a field and chewing on them. They created scientific, exact processes, in which they would produce drugs via “dehumidifaction/dessication, grinding, squeezing or boiling of the plants' roots with a formation of a juice, oil or mush extract”. They would often add wine to the plants’ opus to enhance the effect.

segments.titre: Yanghai Tombs: 789 grams of high-THC cannabis
segments.resume: A 2,700 year old shaman's grave in the Yanghai Tombs, China held almost 2 pounds (789 grams) of cannabis, at first mistaken for coriander. Its THC concentration was higher than wild plants of the time, though below today's, suggesting the Gushi culture cultivated cannabis to get high.
segments.texte: So what was one of the first ever discovered uses of drugs that are still around and used today? Cannabis was found in a 2,700 year old grave in the Yanghai Tombs, China. Not just cannabis. Almost 2 pounds (789 grams) of weed. Found in a single grave, that of an ancient shaman. There was so much, archaeologists initially assumed it was coriander or something else that would be used for cooking or burning. The most shocking part of the discovery came after the cannabis had been analyzed. While cannabinoid plants had been found at other ancient sites, the concentration of tetrahydrocannabinol in those finds - more commonly known as THC - was equal to the low THC concentration of such plants that were growing wild at the time. The Yanghai Tombs discovery was different. The cannabis archaeologists found here had a much higher THC concentration than wild plants of the time. Though still not up to the high concentrations found today, it suggested that the Gushi culture the tombs belonged to was actively cultivating cannabis in order to get high.

segments.titre: Burned with incense and spread along the Silk Road
segments.resume: Cannabis was probably burned with incense in a small closed space and the vapors inhaled, not smoked as today. Because the region lay on the Silk Road, the find marks both the start of purposeful use and its spread, as archaeobotanist Robert Spengler notes.
segments.texte: Back then, it would not have been ingested the same way it was today. Instead of being smoked, it would have been burned alongside incense in a small, closed space. People who wanted to get high would gather and inhale the vapors. Why does that matter so much? Because we may be looking at the first use of weed by ancient people to get high; but also because, while the area is remote today, it used to be around the Silk Road. One of the biggest and most important trade routes in the ancient world. This find not only marks the start of people purposely high, but the spread of it as well. As archaeobotanist Robert Spengler says, “...that knowledge of cannabis smoking and specific… varieties of the cannabis plant were among the cultural traditions that spread along these exchange routes.”

segments.titre: Conclusion: first drug cultivation and link to Alcohol vs Weed video
segments.resume: Scientists appear to have found the first instance of cultivating a substance still used today, so the modern world is still smoking history. The video closes by asking how bad smoking or drinking really is and pointing to the video Alcohol vs Weed - Which is Actually Worse For You?
segments.texte: It seems like scientists have discovered the first instance of drug cultivation for a substance that survives and thrives today. The modern world didn’t just inherit history… it’s still smoking it. When people want to relax they turn to their drug of choice. But how bad is smoking or drinking really?
